blocks.text: I, who formerly kept the starling and the high-flying Bistonian crane away from the seed (that is, from the grains). Cranes, then, will have been clean by the definition of Aristeas, who counts as clean τῶν πτηνῶν τὰ πυροῖς καὶ ὀσπρίοις χρώμενα πρὸς τὴν τροφὴν [tōn ptēnōn ta pyrois kai ospriois chrōmena pros tēn trophēn], those birds which are nourished on wheat and pulse. What is more, among the ancient Greeks cranes were not only eaten but even counted among the delicacies, especially around Thessaly, where the wealthier had on their estates their own γερανοβοτίας [geranobotias] or γερανοβοσίας [geranobosias], that is, crane pastures, which Pollux mentions, following Plato in the Statesman. And in the Balearic islands the vipio, as they called the smaller crane, was held in honour at table. So Pliny, book 10, ch. 49. The same author wonders why Cornelius Nepos, writing under Augustus, said that storks were preferred to cranes, since this bird is now, he says, sought after among the very first, while no one would want to touch the other. Hence Horace, in the dinner of Nasidienus, at which Maecenas was present, book 2, Satire 8:
— — — — then followed slaves carrying on a great platter the carved limbs of a crane, sprinkled with much salt, not without meal.
And Ovid, treating of the frugality of the ancients, Fasti book 6:

Nor did Latium know the bird that rich Ionia supplies, nor the one that delights in Pygmy blood. [II, 630] That is, the francolin and the crane were not yet among the delicacies of the Romans. And Statius too, in Hercules Vindex, censures thus the gluttons of his own time, whose palate was more learned than was fitting:
Ah, wretches! who delight to know how the bird of the Phasis differs from the wintering crane of Rhodope. — —

So much, then, for the word עגור agor, over which I see that the ancient translators stumbled. In Isaiah, for the words כסוס עגור, like a swallow and agor, that is, a crane, the Greek Elders have only ὡς χελιδὼν [hōs chelidōn], and the Arabic translator مثل سنونوة [mithl sunūnwa] like a swallow, the following word being omitted altogether; and Jerome, Like a young swallow; Aquila, ὡς ἵππος ἀγώρ [hōs hippos agōr]; and Theodotion, ὡς χελιδὼν ἀγὼρ [hōs chelidōn agōr], because they were content to transcribe an unknown word. But the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܣܢܘܢܝܬܐ ܕܡܨܦܪܐ, like a swallow that chatters; and the Chaldee כסוסיא דאחיד, like a swallow that has been caught; with which Symmachus's version agrees, ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλειθεῖσα [hōs chelidōn enkleitheisa], like a swallow shut in; as if they had read סגור sagur instead of עגור agor. But that עגור agor is to be read is shown by Aquila, Symmachus, all the Hebrews, and the comparison of this passage with Ierem. VIII, 7. There again the same words סיס sis and עגור agor are joined, and indeed so joined that it is clear that עגור agor is the name of a bird, like תור thor and סיס sis, which precede it. Jerome renders it stork, and the Greeks ἀγροῦ στρουθία [agrou strouthia]. But ἀγροῦ [agrou] arose from ἀγὼρ [agōr], and στρουθία [strouthia] is a gloss that crept from the margin into the text. The Chaldee and the Syriac very well explain it as ܟܘܪܟܝܐ kurkeja, that is, crane, although not in its proper order, as [col. 80] we noted above ^{(3)}.

Although עגור agor is not used today for the crane among the Arabs, it may nevertheless once have been so used, and may derive from the fact that by the verb عجر [ʿajara] agara they mean that someone returns home by right of return, or flees away, which is most characteristic of cranes. For it is well known that out of love of their homeland they return every year to Scythia and Thrace, where they were born, and indeed τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστον καλιὰν ἀναγνωρίζειν, ὡς τὴν οἰκίαν ἀνθρώπους [tēn heautōn hekaston kalian anagnōrizein, hōs tēn oikian anthrōpous], that each recognizes its own nest, as men do their house: which Aelian sets out at length in book 3, ch. 13 and 23. And perhaps from the same source it came about that the royal couriers were called by the Syrians and Persians Ἄγγαροι [Angaroi], aggari or angari. For the angari were believed to rival cranes in speed of running. Φασί τινες θᾶττον τῶν γεράνων ταύτην τὴν πορείαν ἀνύττειν [Phasi tines thatton tōn geranōn tautēn tēn poreian anyttein] (says Xenophon in book 8 of the Cyropaedia): Some report that this journey is accomplished faster than the flight of cranes. [II, 631] That the running of the angari is treated there will be clear to anyone who reads the passage. Among the Cypriots, however, agor was a bird very different from the crane, namely the eagle, if we believe these words of Hesychius: Ἀγώρ· ἀετὸς, Κύπριοι [Agōr: aetos, Kyprioi]. But perhaps it had been written Ἀγώρ· γερανός [Agōr: geranos]; and, the first part of the word γερανὸς [geranos] having been omitted because of its similar ending to the preceding word, ἀετός [aetos] was made out of ἀνὸς [anos] ^{(4)}.
